posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Here is a new thought/twist on an old idea I had. 

Make a series of sqished 2D images onto a high resolution film with a white light source in a modified enlarger. After each frame is recorded the cylindrical lens in the enlarger is tilted to move the focused, squished image to the next slit area on the film. Once the film has been fully exposed process with high contrast developer as you would Black and White film. Then place the film with all the slits onto holographic table. Have an array of cylindrical lenses matching in size to the slits. Then a focusing lens to overlap the images onto the holgoraphic plate. Expose all at one time.

![Image](http://www.sketchys.com/HoloPage/HoloFiles/Illustrations/MultiOneStep.jpg)

Summarizing; I want to take a series of slit images that are reconded on a high resolution silver halide film. How I get them there is what I am trying to work out. These are standard squished flat images not holographic images. Then I wish to use some type of focusing system to take each image on each slit and focus it to the same overlapping spot in space. Simple right?....

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
You will probably get distortions. The way the cylindrical lens is rotating will probably create coma, at least, if not astigmatism. Also, the slit width will not be constant, which in turn, will cause effects similar to pincushion or barrel distortion in the hologram.

What's the purpose of the cylindrical lens array? The light from the high res film seems to be going straight through the lens array with no change power.

The "math" is fairly easy. It's effectively a two-lens imaging system. In practice, you have to be careful with multi-lens systems because the focal length of one lens may be within another piece of equipment. In this case, you cannot physically place a second lens. 

There are many lens design programs that'll enable you to calculate all this without any need for hand calculations. I think I've got a sample from some convention, which will enable you to at least see if it's feasible. Even though you may not be able to save, you may be able to print out the various lens parameters. If you're interested email me and I'll try and find it.

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md: Isn't this idea essentially making a hologram of a lenticular image? You can transilluminate a lenticular photograph, and project it (through a large diameter lens) onto a recording plane and get the same result. For that matter, just make a Denisyuk type recording of a lenticular photograph.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Yes Bob, I think it would be very close to that. But the standard lenticular images do not "squish" the image if I am correct. The only take slices of it and alternate the sliced thought the final image. And may be limited to just a few "different" images. 

One may achive a nice 3D effect with the lenticular though, even if it has virtually no paralax or animation.

Dinesh has experience with lenticulars and may wish to comment. I know very little about lenticulars.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md: Actually, you can get quite a lot of parallax and motion. In full colour, no less! I've always thought that lenticulars were a serious alternative to holograms, since they're cheaper, faster to produce and create full colour, images with more paralax than in most H1/H2 setups. Having said that, it can't beat the parallax of a Denisyuk.
